sections.label: Singapore safety and crime rate
sections.summary: In 2020, 97% of Singapore residents felt safe walking alone at night, and in 2021 the overall crime rate was 355 cases per 100,000 population excluding cyber crimes.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: In the 2020 Gallup Global Law and Order Report, 97% of Singapore residents feel safe walking alone on the streets at night.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: In 2021, Singapore's overall crime rate was 355 cases per 100,000 population excluding cyber crimes.

sections.label: DNA profile matches and unmatched samples
sections.summary: In 2021, about 800 DNA profile matches were made, but approximately 60% of crime scene samples collected from 2017 to 2021 were unmatched against the DNA database.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: In 2021, the number of matches to DNA profiles derived from crime scene samples was about 800.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: However, a large proportion of Police's crime scene samples, approximately 60% of crime scene samples collected between 2017 and 2021, were unmatched when screened against our DNA database.

sections.label: Prior convictions of registrable crime offenders
sections.summary: About one in three individuals convicted of a registrable crime between 2017 and 2021 had a previous conviction for a non-registrable crime.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Our statistics show that about one in three individuals convicted of a registrable crime between 2017 and 2021, had been previously convicted of a non-registrable crime.

sections.label: Expanding DNA collection to non-registrable crimes
sections.summary: England collects DNA for imprisonable and some non-imprisonable offences, so it is proposed to expand DNA collection to non-registrable crimes punishable with imprisonment and not compoundable, unless specified in the Fourth Schedule.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: England collects DNA information for imprisonable offences and some non-imprisonable offences.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Therefore, we propose to expand the scope of crimes eligible for the collection of DNA information and identifying information, to include non-registrable crimes which fulfil two criteria.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: One, they are punishable with imprisonment; and two, they are not compoundable under any written law, unless the offence is specified in the third column of the Fourth Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code 2010.

sections.label: Penalty for refusing fingerprints or samples
sections.summary: Refusing without reasonable excuse to allow fingerprints or a body sample to be taken is an offence punishable by a fine up to $1,000, imprisonment up to one month, or both.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Currently, if an individual refuses, without reasonable excuse, to allow his fingerprints or a body sample to be taken, he is guilty of an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $1,000, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one month, or both.

sections.label: Expanding DNA uses and foreign sharing
sections.summary: Clause 6 inserts a new section 32 to expand prescribed uses of DNA information to three public interest categories, and Clause 10 amends section 13I to let Police share DNA information of individuals convicted of registrable crimes with foreign law enforcement agencies.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Clause 6 inserts a new section 32 to expand the prescribed uses of DNA information to three new categories that are in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Next, Clause 10 amends section 13I, which will be renumbered to section 47 by clause 9, to give the Police the discretion to share DNA information of an individual convicted of a registrable crime, with foreign law enforcement agencies for investigations and proceedings, where it is appropriate to do so.

sections.label: DNA crime scene sample matches
sections.summary: In 2021 about 800 crime scene samples matched DNA profiles, while roughly 60% of samples from 2017 to 2021 were unmatched.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: In 2021, the number of matches to DNA profiles derived from crime scene samples was about 800.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: However, a large proportion of Police’s crime scene samples, approximately 60% of crime scene samples collected between 2017 and 2021, were unmatched when screened against our DNA database.

sections.label: Bill's four DNA amendments
sections.summary: The Bill proposes four amendments: expanding collection and uses of DNA information, strengthening protection, and introducing removal procedures.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: Conversely, a smaller pool of DNA data would be less effective in helping the Police solve crimes.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: This Bill proposes four key amendments: first, expand the scope for the collection of DNA information and other identifying information; second, expand the prescribed uses of DNA information; third, strengthen the protection of DNA information; and fourth, introduce procedures to allow the removal of information in the databases.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
sentences.text: The proposed amendments to the Registration of Criminals Act will enable law enforcement agencies to carry out their duties more effectively, to ensure the safety and security of Singapore, while balancing these expanded powers against individuals’ right to privacy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Individuals under investigation for both registrable and less serious eligible crimes are expected to surrender their DNA to the Police.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To the extent that this Bill is aimed at cracking cases and bringing criminals to justice, the Workers' Party supports the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Apart from widening the scope of crimes that requires the surrender of one's DNA, the Bill also introduces procedures to allow for the removal of DNA information from the Police's DNA database and strengthens the protection of DNA and non-DNA identifying records.

sections.label: Question on DNA database secrecy
sections.summary: A question asks the Minister to elaborate on how the secrecy of the DNA database will be ensured.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: First, could the Minister elaborate how the secrecy of the DNA database will be ensured?

sections.label: Screening and logging database access
sections.summary: The Ministry's press release states that all persons accessing the DNA database must be screened and authorised, with access logged and recorded.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Ministry's press release on the First Reading of this Bill dated 1 August states that all persons accessing the DNA database will have to be screened and authorised by the Police with all access logged and recorded, in addition to a tamper proof audit trail to detect data modification.

sections.label: Proposed section 32 catch-all clause
sections.summary: Proposed section 32(h) is a catch-all clause allowing DNA information to be used for any prescribed purpose.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Paragraphs (b) to (g) of the proposed section 32 aim to narrow the remit of the use of DNA information solely for criminal analysis and investigations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, the proposed section 32(h) is a catch-all clause that states that DNA information can be used for any purpose that may be prescribed.

sections.label: Bill's unascertained financial expenditure
sections.summary: The note states the Bill will involve the Government in extra financial expenditure, the exact amount not presently ascertainable.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The note states that this Bill will involve the Government in extra financial expenditure, the exact amount of which cannot at present be ascertained.

sections.label: Cost of taking DNA samples
sections.summary: The question asks how much taking each DNA sample from an accused or convicted person costs the taxpayer today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Specifically, I would like to ask how much the taking of each DNA sample from an accused or convicted person costs the taxpayer today.

sections.label: Unmatched crime scene DNA samples
sections.summary: The speaker hopes the Bill reduces the percentage of unmatched DNA samples from crime scenes, currently 60%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Once this Bill is passed, it is my hope that the percentage of unmatched DNA samples from scenes of crime, currently running at 60%, would be reduced.

sections.label: Deletion of accused DNA information
sections.summary: Currently an accused's identifying and DNA information is automatically deleted within three months of acquittal or discharge; the proposal requires the accused to apply for removal.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Currently, the identifying and DNA information of an accused person will automatically be deleted within three months from the accused's acquittal or discharge.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: It is proposed that instead of an automatic deletion, the accused has to apply for the removal.

sections.label: DNA database removal and retention
sections.summary: Removal from the electronic DNA database equals destruction of a physical record, and the Bill changes the default from automatic deletion to automatic retention.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: As the DNA information is stored in electronic form in the DNA database, removal of the information from the database is equivalent to the destruction of a physical record like a photograph."  My question to the hon Minister of State is as follows: the current Bill changes the default from automatic deletion to automatic retention.

sections.label: Magistrate referral for blood samples
sections.summary: The passage cites a 2002 statement on court-ordered blood samples and notes the Bill proposes removing referral to the Magistrate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: In this regard, I again wish to highlight that in 2002, the hon Minister for Home Affairs then, Mr Wong Kan Seng stated as follows, "But if the suspect refuses to give that consent, he can be brought to Court and the Court may order him to provide the blood sample, and if he still refuses, of course, appropriate warning will be given and inference will be drawn by the Court for his refusal to provide that blood sample." In this Bill, it is proposed that the referral to the Magistrate is to be taken away.

sections.label: Protections and wider police DNA powers
sections.summary: The protections cover individual privacy, personal data collected and the vulnerable, while granting Police more power over DNA and non-DNA data through a wider scope of offences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: These are to protect (a) individual privacy; (b) personal data collected; and (c) the vulnerable.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: This is done by granting more power to the Police to collect DNA and non-DNA data of offenders, through a much wider scope of offences; in fact, a list of even less serious offences.

sections.label: DNA data removal after acquittal
sections.summary: Acquitted, discharged or compounded individuals must now apply to Police to remove their DNA and non-DNA data, with appeals to a Reviewing Tribunal.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Today, the Police are required to immediately remove both DNA and non-DNA data from the database when an individual is acquitted, discharged or the offence is compounded.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: But with the amendments, such individuals will now have to apply to the Police to remove their data.

sentences.speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: If rejected, one will then have to appeal to a Reviewing Tribunal.

sections.label: Registration of Criminals Amendment Bill
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Registration of Criminals (Amendment) Bill, which expands and enhances collection of DNA and non-DNA identifying information.

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Will the second murder of the 10-year-old child by Adrian Lim and his partners be avoided, or will the perpetrator that killed the four children from the Tan family be apprehended?

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: These questions are pertinent today, as I rise to speak in support of the Registration of Criminals (Amendment) Bill, which expands and enhances the collection of DNA and non-DNA identifying information.

sections.label: Reckless driving as eligible crime
sections.summary: MHA listed reckless or dangerous driving causing hurt as one of the eligible crimes under the amendment Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: MHA has further listed that reckless or dangerous driving causing hurt is one of the eligible crimes under the amendment Bill.

sections.label: Drivers with lower blameworthiness
sections.summary: The speaker says drivers who unintentionally cause hurt or minimal or no injury should not have their DNA information collected.

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Although I stand firm that they should be dealt with fairly under our laws, drivers who unintentionally cause hurt or minimal or no injury, in my view, should not be subject to having their DNA information collected as the degree of blameworthiness of their actions is lower.

sections.label: Oklahoma City DNA data breach
sections.summary: In November 2021, a laboratory processing DNA evidence for Oklahoma City Police suffered a data breach exposing sexual assault victims' personal data.

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In November 2021, a laboratory that was processing DNA evidence from rape victims for the Oklahoma City Police Department (OKCPD) in the United States was involved in a data breach due to unauthorised third-party access to their network, resulting in the exposure of personal data of an unknown number of victims of sexual assault.

sections.label: Questions on DNA database safeguards
sections.summary: The speaker asks MHA to outline legislative safeguards, database access controls, breach response plans, and cites low DNA match rates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Although there was an assurance that legislative safeguards will be introduced with several examples cited in MHA’s press release, I did not manage to find them within the amendment Bill.

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Thus, I would like to ask if MHA can outline some of the legislative safeguards, such as whether the data will be stored in an on-premises secured database at a secured location or a secured cloud database.

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Also, how will the access of the database be controlled, that is, who are the people that MHA has identified to access the database based on their needs for investigation?

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Thirdly, will there be a data breach response plan in the unfortunate event that the DNA database experiences a data breach?

sentences.speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Although the Police have a high solving rate for murder cases through DNA information, according to Lianhe Zaobao, between 2017 and 2021, about 60% of the DNA samples collected by the Police at the crime scene did not match the existing database.

sections.label: DNA collection after discharge outcomes
sections.summary: Accused persons with a discharge amounting to an acquittal will not have DNA collected, while those with a discharge not amounting to an acquittal will.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Three, my understanding is that accused persons who receive a judgment of a discharge amounting to an acquittal (DATA) will not have their DNA collected but those who are discharged not amounting to an acquittal (DNAQ) will have their DNA collected.

sections.label: Rationale for broad registrable offences approach
sections.summary: The question asks MHA's rationale for a broad sweeping approach, noting some registrable offences are petty and some more severe.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: As some registrable offences may be petty in nature and some being more severe, what is MHA's rationale in deciding of this very broad sweeping approach?

sections.label: DNA sharing with foreign agencies
sections.summary: The question asks whether DNA information may be shared with law enforcement agencies outside Singapore, such as through INTERPOL or extraterritorial laws.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Two, will there be any chance where this DNA information will be shared with law enforcement agencies outside of Singapore as part of worldwide police investigations, for example, as part of INTERPOL or for laws with extraterritorial effects?

sections.label: Support for expanding DNA collection
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Bill despite queries and the need for safeguards, saying it will expand collection and use of identifying and DNA information.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the above queries and the need for safeguards, I support this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: This Bill will expand the collection and use of identifying information and DNA information.

sections.label: Force for non-invasive body samples
sections.summary: Under new section 25, if an individual refuses to give a non-invasive body sample, a DNA officer may use force to take it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Under the new section 25, if an individual refuses to give a body sample that is not an invasive sample, a DNA officer may use force to take that body sample.

sections.label: Data retention after acquittal or compounding
sections.summary: With the amendments, the default position is that data will be retained for individuals acquitted, granted a discharge amounting to an acquittal, or whose offence was compounded.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: With the amendments, the default position is that the data will be retained for individuals who have been acquitted, granted a discharge amounting to an acquittal or had their offence compounded.

sections.label: Removing information after rejected application
sections.summary: The speaker says information should be removed without a fresh application if an earlier section 39 rejection reason no longer holds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In my view, the default action should be to remove someone's information without a fresh application if the individual was earlier rejected due to a section 39 reason and the reason no longer holds.

sections.label: Police blood sample DNA collection
sections.summary: A key amendment lets Police officers instruct a suspect to provide blood samples for DNA collection without a Magistrate's order.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: A key amendment is to allow Police officers to instruct a suspect to provide blood samples to collect DNA, without the need for a Magistrate's order.

sections.label: Default expungement of suspects' information
sections.summary: The Member asks the Minister of State to clarify the rationale for default expungement of suspects' information in No Further Action cases under clause 35(3).

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Regarding the retention of information, as the intent of this Bill is to collect more data to improve investigations, can the Minister of State clarify the rationale for the default expungement of suspects' information in cases of No Further Action under clause 35(3)?

sections.label: Sharing DNA information of convicted persons
sections.summary: The Member asks whether criteria for assessing necessity of sharing DNA information will be more stringent than currently, given DNA is more sensitive than fingerprints.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding that these persons have been convicted, given that DNA information is more sensitive compared to fingerprints, can the Minister of State clarify if criteria to assess necessity for sharing will be made more stringent than currently?

sections.label: Data security safeguards and enhancements
sections.summary: The Member asks the Minister of State to clarify existing data security safeguards, their effectiveness, and proposed enhancements to be put in place.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Given this, can the Minister of State clarify the existing data security safeguards, their effectiveness and proposed enhancements that are implemented and, therefore, to be put in place to provide greater public assurance?

sections.label: Voluntary DNA and refusal penalties
sections.summary: The Member welcomes voluntary DNA provision with deletion on request, and supports fines or jail for accused who refuse blood samples without reasonable excuse.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: As such, I welcome a key amendment in the Bill which includes allowing individuals to provide his DNA or non-DNA identifying information voluntarily to Police.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Critically, volunteers can request the Police to delete their information at any time and the Police must accede to their request.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Additionally, due to the high success probability of solving crimes and the possibility to exonerate the innocent, I am in support of the fine and/or jail term that will be introduced for accused individuals who refuse to provide blood samples without a reasonable excuse.

sections.label: DNA database relatives safeguards
sections.summary: A Cell Reports study showed DNA sequences may be similar, raising the question of safeguards for relatives or possible doppelgangers on the database.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: A recent study published in the journal Cell Reports has shown that their DNA sequence may be similar.

sentences.speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
sentences.text: Thus, what are the safeguards for the relatives of people or possible doppelgangers who are on the database?

sections.label: Expanding DNA database privacy
sections.summary: DNA extraction has improved Police apprehension odds, and expanding the database to eligible crimes would increase effectiveness, but citizen privacy protection must be ensured.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
sentences.text: The ability to extract DNA from the crime scene and run it through the database has greatly improved the odds of the Police here in apprehending criminals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
sentences.text: There is certainly merit in expanding the database to include "eligible" crimes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
sentences.text: A larger database would exponentially increase the effectiveness of the Police Force in solving cases, especially when such cases have little leads, such as a lack of CCTV footage or eyewitnesses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
sentences.text: However, with the ability to collect DNA from more suspects and offenders, how do we ensure the privacy of our citizens is adequately protected?

sections.label: Acquitted suspects DNA removal
sections.summary: The passage asks how long acquitted, discharged or uninvolved suspects have to apply for removal of their DNA information.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
sentences.text: Consequently, for suspects acquitted of the crimes, discharged by the Court or found not to be involved in a crime, how long does the individual have to apply for his DNA information to be removed?

sections.label: Capacity for DNA samples
sections.summary: The passage asks whether there is necessary capacity to handle the expected influx of DNA samples as evidence given the extensive eligible offences list.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha
sentences.text: As the list of "eligible offences" is quite extensive, do we have the necessary capacity to handle the expected influx of DNA samples as evidence?

sections.label: Support expanding Police DNA powers
sections.summary: The speaker supports expanding Police powers to collect DNA and non-DNA identifying information for registrable and eligible crimes, including drink driving, public fighting and voluntarily causing hurt.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: One would never know how such data may be needed to help solve crimes which could potentially impact anyone of us.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Hence, I support the proposals to expand the powers of the Police to collect DNA and non-DNA identifying information for both registrable crimes and "eligible crimes".

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The wider scope of eligible crimes will include drink driving, fighting in public and voluntarily causing hurt.

sections.label: Verification delays and civil use
sections.summary: The Ministry should address verification delays from power outages, and the Minister should consider permitting civil use by relevant individuals with independent Court approval.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The Ministry should also address the potential problem where there could be delays in verification due to situations such as power outages.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: I also appeal to the Minister to consider permitting civil use by relevant individuals, with the approval of an independent Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: (In Mandarin):   This Registration of Criminal (Amendment) Bill includes the DNA of persons who have committed eligible non-registrable offences in the scope of data collection.

sections.label: Support for DNA collection Bill
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Bill to enhance DNA collection by law enforcement agencies while ensuring safeguards for personal data.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Therefore, this Bill is to take precautionary measures to prevent minor problems from happening.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: I stand in support of the Bill, which seeks to enhance DNA collection by our law enforcement agencies, as this will allow our Police officers to better carry out their duties and ensure the safety and security of Singapore and Singaporeans while also ensuring that sufficient safeguards for personal data are in place.

sections.label: Expanding DNA collection scope
sections.summary: The speaker supports expanding the scope of crimes where DNA and other identifying information can be collected.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: DNA analysis is but a single tool in the Police's toolbox of crime-solving methods, which include non-DNA identifying information, CCTV analytics and ground interviews.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: I, therefore, fully support the proposal to expand the scope of crimes where DNA and other identifying information can be collected so as to help the Police solve crimes more efficiently and more effectively.

sections.label: Call for national DNA registry
sections.summary: The speaker calls for a fundamental review and consideration of a national DNA registry for all Singaporeans and residents.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: Lastly, Mdm Deputy Speaker, while I note that the intent of today's Bill is to debate the circumstances in which our law enforcement agencies can collect DNA and non-DNA identifying information, I would like to call for a more fundamental review on whether we should do more than just limit DNA collection only to criminals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: We should seriously consider establishing a national DNA registry where every Singaporean and resident would be required to log our DNA sequence.

sections.label: Hope for national DNA registry
sections.summary: The speaker believes there is space to collect DNA from more people and hopes for a national DNA registry.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: However, I believe there is space for us to do more – to be able to collect DNA from more people and for more uses beyond just identifying criminals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
sentences.text: I also hope that, one day, we could have a national DNA registry as an added tool in our Police's crime-solving arsenal.

sections.label: Road Traffic Act DNA eligibility
sections.summary: The passage states which reckless or dangerous driving and driving without due care offences allow Police DNA collection.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: The offence of reckless or dangerous driving under section 64 of the Road Traffic Act 1961 is an eligible crime if no death or grievous hurt is caused.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: As for the offence of driving without due care, under section 65 of the same Act, the offence is a registrable crime if death or grievous hurt is caused.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: If no death or grievous hurt is caused, the offence of driving without due care is compoundable and, hence, Police will not be able to collect the DNA information of offenders.

sections.label: Other jurisdictions DNA collection
sections.summary: South Australia and England collect DNA information for all imprisonable offences, and England also for some non-imprisonable offences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: For instance, South Australia collects DNA information for all imprisonable offences while England collects DNA information for all imprisonable offences and some non-imprisonable offences.

sections.label: Conditions for taking body sample
sections.summary: A body sample may be taken if consent is refused or unavailable, the volunteer agrees, and a Magistrate sanctions it.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: First, the parent or guardian's consent is refused without good cause or cannot be obtained despite all reasonable efforts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: Second, the volunteer is willing to give the body sample, and third, a Magistrate's sanction is obtained.

sections.label: Police force for non-invasive samples
sections.summary: Police officers are empowered to use reasonable force to obtain non-invasive samples such as buccal swabs to solve crimes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: A guilty criminal may not consent to provide data for fear of being incriminated and time is often of the essence when solving a crime.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: We must thus empower our Police officers to use reasonable force to obtain non-invasive samples, such as buccal swabs, in order to solve crimes.

sections.label: Duplicate independent sample processing
sections.summary: The sample is independently processed in duplicate at separate times to ensure the integrity of the DNA profile.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: Thereafter, the sample will be independently processed in duplicate at separate times to ensure the integrity of the DNA profile derived from the sample.

sections.label: RCA DNA use and disclosure limits
sections.summary: DNA information collected under the RCA may only be used for RCA purposes and not disclosed to private organisations or civil proceedings.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: DNA information collected under the RCA can only be used for the purposes specified under the RCA.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: DNA information collected under the RCA may not be disclosed to private organisations or used in civil proceedings.

sections.label: Online application to Registrar
sections.summary: An applicant applies to the Registrar online with particulars and case details, and the Registrar replies officially within 30 days.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: One only has to apply to the Registrar online, with his particulars and case details.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: The Registrar will review the application and provide an official reply within 30 days.

sections.label: Discharge and stern warning applicants
sections.summary: Individuals given a discharge not amounting to an acquittal or a stern warning will not be allowed to apply for removal of their information.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Patrick Tay asked whether individuals who are granted a discharge not amounting to an acquittal or given a stern warning can apply for their information to be removed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: These individuals will not be allowed to apply for their information to be removed.

sections.label: Retention of police DNA information
sections.summary: His identifying and DNA information will continue to be retained by the Police as it may be vital for solving future crimes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: On the other hand, his identifying information and DNA information will continue to be retained by the Police, as this information may be vital for solving future crimes.

sections.label: DNA database access restriction
sections.summary: Only authorised individuals are allowed to access the DNA database.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: Only authorised individuals are allowed to access the DNA database.

sections.label: Bill and law enforcement effectiveness
sections.summary: Assessing cost involves factors like officers involved and salaries, and the Bill will enable law enforcement agencies to carry out duties more effectively and keep Singapore safe and secure.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: If we wanted to identify the cost, technically, one will have to assess the number of officers involved, the time cost based on their salaries and so on and many other factors to do this exercise.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: This Bill will enable our law enforcement agencies to carry out their duties more effectively and to continue to keep Singapore safe and secure.

sections.label: CLTPA and MDA retention clauses
sections.summary: CLTPA and the Misuse of Drugs Act have clauses on taking and retaining photographs, finger impressions and body samples, so there is no need to consolidate them under the RCA.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: On Member's second question, I would like to share that under CLTPA as well as the Misuse of Drugs Act, there are clauses that specify with regards to the taking of photographs, finger impressions, body samples, so on and so forth as well as with regards to the retention of these photographs, finger impressions as well as body samples.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: As such, because they are already explicitly stated in the CLTPA as well as the MDA, we do not see a need for us to consolidate them under the RCA.

sections.label: Blood samples and mental capacity
sections.summary: For individuals above 16 years old whom the Police assess may lack mental capacity to give consent, the Police will err on the side of caution and not take an invasive blood sample.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: On the first part, with regard to individuals who are above 16 years old, where the Police assessed that the individual may not have the mental capacity to give consent, the Police will err on the side of caution and not take an invasive blood sample.

sections.label: Police vernacular language ability
sections.summary: In most situations, Police officers are able to speak in the vernacular.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
sentences.text: In most situations, our Police officers are able to speak in the vernacular.
